rows.description:
Operator-ratified direction (sitting tk-gn3hrkv on tk-xexv7bo, 2026-10-19). The pack re-expresses each feature on upstream primitives or drops it; target is ~25-35k lines (roughly 75-80% below today's ~130k operational), with judgment in prompts, flow in formulas, mechanics in the platform.

The four tests every member and every review applies:
1. Prose and config are free — prompts, skills, checklists, formulas, orders, work queries.
2. A pack noun requires a dated warrant naming the missing platform primitive and a retirement trigger — when upstream ships the primitive, migrating onto it is scheduled work, and a converter between a pack noun and a platform noun is the missed-trigger alarm.
3. Glue composes native calls but may not add semantics native mechanisms already express (leases, assignment, groups, waits). One call wrapping a series of steps for consistency and agent-context economy is legal glue (gctk's intent).
4. Surfaces render platform objects, never mint their own.

Gap protocol: a claim that upstream cannot express X is recorded dated, re-verified against current upstream docs before it justifies anything, and answered by re-expressing or reshaping the feature — never by a wrapper, a fork, or an upstream campaign.

Full evaluation record and converse anatomy: tk-xexv7bo notes (2026-10-19). Members migrate one feature each. Sequencing: the foundation rule lands first, the docs split clears what agents learn from, the converse migration sets the pattern.

metadata.epic_hypothesis: For the operator, who reviews the city's changes, and the agents who change gc-toolkit, moving each pack feature onto the primitive Gas City ships, or dropping it, will move their effort from repairing the pack's own machinery to the product; the signal is that fixes fall from over half of the changes merged to main (214 of 398 in October) to under a quarter.
metadata.epic_indicators: The pack's runtime (code, flow and text) as tools/measure.sh counts it on main, re-measured as each lane member lands: 114.8k at the 10-31 baseline, 115.9k on 2026-11-06, against a built-once estimate of 35.0k.
metadata.epic_ruling_reason: The operator confirmed this hypothesis in conversation tk-ij23o7p on 2026-11-06, answering a hand-back that quoted the sentence word for word: "Sure, we can go with this." Recorded on 2026-11-08 under the operator's ruling in conversation tk-nxb4z05, which gives a hypothesis they have confirmed its continue ruling.

rows.description:
Landing [another rig]'s untrack PR now takes bd down on that rig until a reload: land it by hand, or have the sync stop first?

The reset repair this bug reports is gone: a diverged checkout now keeps the file and asks a person. Its close brief also asked me to confirm the sync deletes no file, and the plain fast-forward does delete one, so I left the bug open for you.

You approved the sync cut (PR #1423), whose brief named that cost in general terms and named no live case. One exists: [another rig]'s PR #642, waiting on your review since 10-17, stops tracking .beads/metadata.json. Its body says "Merging is safe now" and counts on the step the cut removed.

If #642 lands as it stands, the sync stalls and asks a person about the two files git names. Once those are cleared, the next sync deletes metadata.json, which no message names, and every bd call on that rig fails with "no beads database found" until [another rig]'s next config reload writes the file back. On 11-06 reloads came at most 1h53 apart until 19:10 MST, with none in the 3h20 since. No beads are lost. I replayed this on a clone of the real repo; the write-back I read in [another rig]'s code and did not run.

1. Close this bug and land #642 by hand (my recommendation). The sync stays as you approved it. Whoever clears that stall runs a short recipe, tested on the same clone and kept in the notes of #642's bead ([another rig's bead]). Skipping it costs the outage above. Any later landing that stops tracking a clean file needs the same care, and [another rig] tracks this same file today.

2. Have the sync stop and ask before it deletes a file the incoming tree ignores, then close this bug. Every later case reaches a person before the file goes, and that person still carries it by hand. It puts about 70 lines plus tests back into the script you just cut.

Until you answer, this bug waits here and #642 stays mergeable with the landing above. Evidence: this bug's notes (tk-9hs7mxv).

rows.description:
**Handle.** Scripts move into gctk.

**Hypothesis.** For the operator and the agents who change gc-toolkit,
rebuilding its logic in gctk makes the pack supportable. The logic is organized
as domains that each own their state, keys and questions, reached through one
CLI where every intent is one `gctk <domain> <verb>` call. The signal is that a
change to one concept touches one place, and no defect comes from two places
disagreeing on a key or a rule.

## Belongs

- gctk's architecture:
  - the CLI, designed from the outside in;
  - the domains that design reveals, each owning its state, the only writers
    of that state, and the questions about it;
  - the ledger, which turns typed fields into keys and back;
  - one adapter per outside system, each with a fake.
- Moving each domain out of shell whole. That includes its keys, its writers,
  its questions and every caller: formulas, prompts, orders, doctor checks and
  the helm board.
- The gctk rig gate and the check-runner cutover (tk-kpanfqm, tk-b0ww25t), and
  the merged gctk rig work (tk-1hazlo2).
- The per-pass snapshot (tk-8gradm4.1), where the structure calls for it.
- Retiring each script, its test suite and its bridge once its intents are
  direct gctk calls. The direction is an assets/scripts that is gone.

## Boundaries

- Same behavior wherever today's copies agree. Where they disagree, the design
  picks one rule and lists every answer that changes, for the operator to
  approve. Nothing is removed to pass a check.
- Speed is a backstop, not the goal. No refinery pass gets slower than today's.
- Not the helm board's UX, which the Helm UX epic (tk-ikpyzn) owns. Helm's
  reads are in scope as a caller.
- Not [another rig]. gctk builds on the store's own rules, and a supervisor route
  gctk lacks is a [another rig] bead the work waits on.
- Not prompt or formula wording, beyond swapping a call site.

## Closure condition

Each check fails today. The baselines come from the 2026-10-16 census.

1. Every metadata key is declared once, by the domain that owns it, and nothing
   outside that domain writes it. Today 49 keys have more than one writer, and
   76 files write metadata.
2. No code outside the ledger spells a key name: no script, formula, prompt,
   doctor check or Go package. Today 169 of the 265 keys in use are spelled in
   more than one file.
3. Each shared question is one function its owner exports, and every caller
   uses it, the board included. Today "blocked" alone is decided in about 78
   places by about 34 rules.
4. Only adapters touch outside systems, and CI runs gctk's Go tests against
   their fakes on every PR. Today CI runs only the shell suites.
5. No caller needs a script to turn intent into action: every formula, prompt,
   order and doctor check acts through a direct gctk call. Today 133 scripts in
   assets/scripts have live callers.
6. Graded at each Epic Checkpoint: the operator picks a recent change to a
   moved domain and judges whether it touched one place and reads clearly.

## Leading indicators

- For each moved domain, the number of places that spell its keys or decide
  its rules, falling to one.
- Defects filed because two places disagreed on a key or a rule.

## Features

- First: tk-ssm8qns.1. It designs gctk's domains from its CLI and proves them
  on "is this blocked?". Each queued port and the cobra bead wait on it, and
  its design rules on them.

## Sequencing (operator, 2026-10-15)

This epic runs after the open-PR landing push and the critical work, while the
rest of gc-toolkit slows down. It stays parked until then, by a blocks edge to
tk-u5t8h6x.

rows.description:
Follow-on increment to the epic-steward v1 (tk-isd5sa / PR#977), from converse sitting tk-089mt7x. Builds the proactive layer that v1 deliberately omits.

## Scope
- Feature level: a bounded delivery window under an epic (SAFe sense), grouping stories (each a PR or few).
- Epic Checkpoint: after a Feature lands, an operator-judged sitting evaluates the epic against its hypothesis and rules continue / shift / close (continue & shift non-terminal, aim the next Feature; close terminal with a reason/outcome). The judge is never the worker.
- Goals consolidation: fold the worthwhile goal-primitive ideas (checkpoint shape, judge-isnt-the-worker, measured-vs-graded criteria, anti-gaming invariant) into the Epic contract; unify the verdict vocabulary to continue/shift/close; retire specs/tk-yaor8a as a separate primitive.
- Prove the checkpoint motion by hand first (manual sittings) before growing any steward automation.

## Relation
Part of the epics-as-first-class-citizen initiative (tk-rctkrj). Blocked by v1 (tk-isd5sa): starts once the gate-only v1 lands.

metadata.epic_boundaries: In: the Feature delivery layer, the Epic Checkpoint cadence, and the goals->epics consolidation. Out: the mechanical close-gate itself (that is v1, tk-isd5sa / PR#977).
metadata.epic_hypothesis: Operator-judged Epic Checkpoints after each Feature (a bounded delivery window), ruling continue/shift/close, let multi-unit epics converge visibly without premature machinery.

rows.description:
Aim: the delivery window and the operator-judged Epic Checkpoint after it, run by hand with no new machinery: a Delivery that is filed, shown and closed with what bd and the pack already do with a child epic, a board row that asks for its checkpoint once it lands, and a skill a sitting follows to rule continue, shift or close.
Done when: its Stories, units 1 to 5 and 7 of the Delivery-layer design, have closed. The epic docs state the model, the work skill files into a Delivery, the checkpoint skill and the converse prompt's closes have landed, a landed Delivery's row asks for its checkpoint, no open child epic on file lacks both an `Aim:` line and a hypothesis, and a Story may be story-typed.

The operator's approval of the Delivery-layer design (tk-wmwcdlc.1, PR #1352) aims this Delivery, as section 2 of `specs/tk-wmwcdlc.1/deliveries-and-epic-checkpoints.md` says. It goes to no pool, because its Stories are the work. It closes at the Epic Checkpoint that follows its landing, as one of that ruling's writes (section 4). Unit 6, the checkpoint's machinery, sits under the epic rather than here, so the epic's own checkpoint after this Delivery is one of the two hand runs unit 6 waits for.

rows.description:
The board's web page has grown one change at a time, and the operator's reviews keep finding its design short. On PR #774 (2026-09-19): "still feels like it takes no consideration of usability into mind at all. It's like word vomit on the page, just slightly better organized." On PR #911 (2026-09-30): "As far as usable designs, this is pretty poor. We simply indent titles, that's best practices from 40 years ago." This epic designs the page as a whole and builds that design.

Its first work is the board's design pass (tk-ikpyzn.12): prototype directions the operator reacts to, a ruling that picks one, and the design written down for the build. The pass also carries the spatial-canvas idea of the closed Attention Canvas epic (tk-eemvf) as a direction to re-test, with that epic's plan and design inputs at specs/tk-eemvf/.

The operator asked for this epic on 2026-11-10 (conversation tk-wc5eiy7): "I also want to dive back into the UI design, since it needs more love. Arguably that should be a clean Epic". Their direction for the board, 2026-11-08 (conversation tk-kz6jl3a): "The board should show everything, but it's about how it's presented that makes it guide towards what really needs me. The board needs to give a holistic executive operator like view, but also the ability to then dive into the area of interest and see how it's progressing."

metadata.epic_boundaries: Cut on the board's web page: how it looks and behaves, and the one read that feeds it. In: the design (the operator's Claude Design session and their rulings of 2026-11-11), building it as the board's only web page, and the page's read, which is one read per rig of the bead graph whose every state is the answer of the pack's shared readers and which adds no rule, no stored state and no new concept. Beside it: what the board must tell you about where things stand is tk-ikpyzn's, and what it marks as needing you is tk-99h9ijx's; the page draws both from the shared readers and decides neither. Not its work: the board's direct store reader and its pack-stamped rows, which tk-1tfzr71.24 retires and the command-line board reads until then, and the parity test that holds the Go contract and its hand-written TypeScript mirror equal, which tk-1tfzr71.25 retires. The page reads neither and gives them no new work.
metadata.epic_hypothesis: If the board is designed as a whole, from prototypes you react to, instead of one change at a time, you can read it and get around in it easily; we'll know it worked when board changes stop coming back from your review for how they look and work.
metadata.epic_indicators: Design complaints in the operator's reviews of board changes. Baseline: PR #774 ("word vomit on the page") and PR #911 ("pretty poor"). Bar: the first five board changes after the design is built draw no complaint on a point the design settled.
metadata.epic_ruling_reason: The operator's go on building their own Claude Design export as one pull request that replaces the board's web page and adds its one read (conversation tk-w2hvygn, 2026-11-11). The hypothesis stands; the course and the boundaries change. Shift is this sitting's reading: they did not use the word.
